full_prose_under_review.title: Grounds for Board Discipline and the Credentials It Reaches
full_prose_under_review.topic: Licensure and discipline / Grounds for Board discipline
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: The credentials 247 CMR 10.01 reaches, the grounds in 247 CMR 10.03 covering scope, impairment, lapsed registration, permitting unlicensed activity and failure to cooperate, the definition of conviction in 247 CMR 10.02, out-of-state discipline under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(t) and 10.06(7), and the protected health care carve-out in 247 CMR 10.03(3)
learning_objectives: Name every credential 247 CMR 10.01 places within the Board's disciplinary reach, and say which of them are individual credentials and which are entity credentials.
Explain why the lettered grounds in 247 CMR 10.03 are not an exhaustive statement of what the Board may discipline.
State the five practice grounds in 247 CMR 10.03(1)(f) through (i) and (m) and identify what each one turns on.
Distinguish the exposure of the person who performs an out-of-scope act from that of the licensee who knowingly permits it.
Apply the definition of conviction in 247 CMR 10.02 to dispositions that fall short of a sentence, and state the evidentiary effect a conviction carries before the Board.
Work out when discipline imposed in another jurisdiction supports Massachusetts action, and identify the proviso that gates it.
Explain why failing without cause to cooperate with the Board is assessed separately from the complaint that prompted the request.
State the two qualifiers on the carve-out in 247 CMR 10.03(3) and explain why it overrides the grounds list rather than sitting beside it.

orientation.text: Massachusetts discipline begins with a credential rather than with a person. 247 CMR 10.01 states the purpose of 247 CMR 10.00 as outlining the procedures the Board uses to handle complaints received against Board registrants or licensees, and in the same passage it names what the Board may act against: a registered pharmacist, a pharmacy technician, a pharmacy, a pharmacy department, a wholesale license, and/or a controlled substance registration issued by the Board. The list mixes individual credentials with entity credentials and does not rank them. 247 CMR 10.03(1) says the same thing from the other direction, allowing the Board to impose disciplinary action against an individual or entity licensed or registered by the Board. One episode inside a pharmacy can therefore put more than one credential at risk at the same time, and nothing in either provision requires the Board to choose between them.

The grounds themselves come from two places, and neither place is closed. 247 CMR 10.03(1) lets the Board act on one or more of the grounds for discipline listed in M.G.L. c. 112, § 61 or on one or more of the grounds that follow in the regulation, so the lettered regulatory list sits alongside a statutory list rather than replacing it. 247 CMR 10.03(2) then provides that nothing in 247 CMR 10.03 shall limit the Board's adoption of policies and grounds for discipline through adjudication as well as through rulemaking. Treating the lettered grounds as an exhaustive catalogue, and reasoning that conduct not described there is therefore beyond reach, is the first mistake available in this area.

Five of the lettered grounds describe the ordinary ways practice itself goes wrong, and each is stated without any element of patient harm. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(f) reaches engaging in conduct beyond the authorized scope of a pharmacist, pharmacy intern or pharmacy technician. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(g) reaches practising the profession while the ability to practise is impaired by illness, use of alcohol, drugs, chemicals, or any other type of substance, or as a result of any mental or physical condition. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(h) reaches engaging in abuse or illegal use of prescription drugs or controlled substances. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(i) reaches continuing to practise the profession after a registration is lapsed, suspended or revoked. And 247 CMR 10.03(1)(m) reaches knowingly permitting, aiding or abetting an unlicensed person to perform activities requiring a license or registration.

The last of those five changes who is in the room. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(m) is written from the point of view of the person who permits rather than the person who acts, so a licensee who knowingly lets someone perform work requiring a license or registration has satisfied the ground personally, and that exposure does not wait on any action against whoever did the work. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(f) points the same way from a different angle: it is drafted around the authorized scope of three named roles, so the enquiry is what the role was authorised to do rather than how the episode turned out. Because 247 CMR 10.01 and 247 CMR 10.03(1) reach each credential separately, the permitting licensee, the person who acted and the entity credential can each be considered on their own footing.

247 CMR 10.02 supplies the definitions 247 CMR 10.00 runs on, and the one that decides questions is conviction. It shall include any guilty verdict or finding of guilt and any admission to or finding of sufficient facts to warrant a finding of guilt, regardless of adjudication, a continuance without a finding, and any plea of guilty or nolo contendere, of or to a crime in any jurisdiction, which has been accepted by the court, whether or not a sentence has been imposed. Every feature a licensee is likely to rely on in arguing that no conviction occurred is named inside that definition rather than outside it: that adjudication was withheld, that the case was continued without a finding, that no sentence followed, that the plea was one of nolo contendere, and that the matter arose in another jurisdiction.

The second sentence of the same definition does separate work. A conviction of any person licensed or registered by the Board shall be conclusive evidence of the commission of that crime in any disciplinary proceeding against such person based upon the conviction. Conclusive evidence closes a door. In a proceeding built upon the conviction, the commission of the crime is established by the conviction itself, so an attempt to reargue the underlying facts is answering a question that is no longer open. What the definition settles is the fact of the crime; what it says nothing about is which credential is at stake or which of the grounds in 247 CMR 10.03 the Board is proceeding under.

Conduct outside Massachusetts is reached by two provisions doing different jobs. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(t) makes having been disciplined in another jurisdiction in any way for reasons substantially the same as those set forth in 247 CMR 10.03 a listed ground in its own right. 247 CMR 10.06(7) states the condition on which the Board may act on such an event: disciplinary action taken against a Massachusetts registrant or licensee by another state or jurisdiction in which that person is also registered or licensed may be the basis for initiation by the Board of disciplinary action against the Massachusetts registrant or licensee, provided that the conduct disciplined in another state or jurisdiction constitutes a violation of Massachusetts law. The proviso is the whole of the test. An out-of-state order is a doorway rather than a verdict, and the enquiry it opens is into the conduct, not into the thoroughness of the other board's process or the finality of its appeals.

247 CMR 10.03(1)(q) is the ground that survives the collapse of everything around it. It reaches failing, without cause, to cooperate with any request by the Board to appear before it or to provide requested information; failing to respond to a Board subpoena; and failing to furnish the Board, its investigators or representatives with records, documents, information or testimony to which the Board is legally entitled. Three features of the drafting matter. It covers ordinary requests as well as subpoenas. It names the Board's investigators and representatives alongside the Board, so a request need not come from the Board sitting as a body. And it is a listed ground standing on its own, so it does not rise or fall with the complaint that prompted the request; the qualifier the provision does attach is the phrase without cause.

247 CMR 10.03(3) is drafted to beat the rest of the section rather than to sit beside it. Notwithstanding the grounds for discipline specified in 247 CMR 10.03, no licensee shall be subject to discipline for providing or assisting in providing, or dispensing medication for, reproductive health care services or gender-affirming health care services, as defined at M.G.L. c. 12, § 11I½, or for any conviction, judgment, discipline, or other sanction arising from such health care services. The reach of that second limb is what makes the provision decisive, because it removes not only the underlying care but the foreign conviction, judgment or discipline built upon it, which is precisely the material that 247 CMR 10.03(1)(t) and 247 CMR 10.06(7) would otherwise supply. Two qualifiers travel with the carve-out and both must hold: the services provided would have been lawful in Massachusetts, and they are consistent with standards for good professional practice in Massachusetts.

Two boundaries keep this material in its place. The first is that 247 CMR 10.01 describes 247 CMR 10.00 as outlining the procedures used to handle complaints, so grounds and reach are only the front half of that chapter; how a matter proceeds once a ground exists, what the Board may then impose, and every period attached to any of it belong to the companion treatment of disciplinary process and are deliberately outside the scope declared for this section. The second is that 247 CMR 10.03(1) opens onto the grounds listed in M.G.L. c. 112, § 61 as well as onto its own lettered list, and this section does not enumerate the statutory grounds. It states only what the regulation itself states about them, which is that they are available to the Board alongside the regulatory list.

worked_examples.scenario: A complaint describes one episode at a Massachusetts pharmacy that implicates both the pharmacist on duty and the way the pharmacy itself was run. Counsel for the pharmacy argues that the Board must elect a single target, and that having opened a matter against the individual it may not also proceed against the entity. How should that argument be evaluated?
steps: Start from the credential rather than from the person. 247 CMR 10.01 names a registered pharmacist, a pharmacy technician, a pharmacy, a pharmacy department, a wholesale license and a controlled substance registration issued by the Board as things the Board may take disciplinary action against.

Read 247 CMR 10.03(1) alongside it, which allows the Board to impose disciplinary action against an individual or entity licensed or registered by the Board, putting individual and entity credentials on the same footing.
Look for the election rule counsel relies on. Neither provision says that one episode supports only one action, and neither ranks the listed credentials against each other.
Weigh what 247 CMR 10.03(2) adds, namely that nothing in 247 CMR 10.03 limits the Board's adoption of policies and grounds for discipline through adjudication as well as through rulemaking.
worked_examples.resolution: The argument fails, because the pharmacist's registration and the pharmacy's credential are separate things the Board may act against and the regulation imposes no election between them. The error the scenario invites is treating discipline as an action against a person, when 247 CMR 10.01 frames it as an action against a credential.

worked_examples.scenario: During a staffing shortage a pharmacist on duty knowingly allows another member of staff to perform work that requires a license or registration. Every prescription involved turns out to be correct and no patient is harmed. The pharmacist takes the view that, because nothing went wrong and because somebody else performed the work, only that other person is exposed.
steps: Identify the provision that speaks to the person who permits. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(m) makes it a ground knowingly to permit, aid or abet an unlicensed person to perform activities requiring a license or registration.

Notice that the ground is complete on knowledge and permission. Performing the activity is what the other person did; permitting it is what the pharmacist did, and the provision is addressed to the second of those.
Check 247 CMR 10.03(1)(f) as well, which reaches engaging in conduct beyond the authorized scope of a pharmacist, pharmacy intern or pharmacy technician and is drafted around the scope of the role.
Search both provisions for an outcome element. Neither names patient harm, and neither makes a correct final product a defence to the conduct described.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacist is exposed on the permitting ground independently of anyone else's exposure. The error the scenario invites is double: reading a good outcome as curing a scope violation, and assuming that only the person whose hands performed the act can be reached.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacist resolved a criminal matter in another state by admitting to sufficient facts; the case was continued without a finding and no sentence was imposed. When the Board writes asking her to appear and to provide information, she concludes that the request rests on a misunderstanding and does not reply, reasoning that there is nothing to answer for because there was no conviction.
steps: Test the first assumption against 247 CMR 10.02, which defines conviction to include any admission to or finding of sufficient facts to warrant a finding of guilt, regardless of adjudication, and a continuance without a finding, of or to a crime in any jurisdiction, whether or not a sentence has been imposed.
Observe that each feature she relies on sits inside that definition rather than outside it, and that the definition reaches a crime in any jurisdiction rather than only a Massachusetts one.
Take the silence separately. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(q) makes it a ground to fail, without cause, to cooperate with any request by the Board to appear before it or to provide requested information.

Ask what the cooperation ground depends on. It is a listed ground in its own right, so it is not conditioned on the underlying request proving well founded; the qualifier the provision states is the phrase without cause.
worked_examples.resolution: She is wrong twice, and the second error is the more expensive one, because a failure to cooperate stands as a ground of its own whatever becomes of the matter that prompted the request. The error the scenario invites is treating a disposition short of a sentence as no conviction, and then treating a private belief that a request is misconceived as cause for ignoring it.

worked_examples.scenario: Another jurisdiction has sanctioned a Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist solely for dispensing medication for reproductive health care services. The services would have been lawful in Massachusetts and are consistent with standards for good professional practice here. A proposal is made to open a Massachusetts matter, reasoning that discipline in another jurisdiction is a listed ground.
steps: Run the out-of-state analysis first, since that is what is being invoked. 247 CMR 10.06(7) permits initiation on the basis of another jurisdiction's discipline provided that the conduct disciplined there constitutes a violation of Massachusetts law, and 247 CMR 10.03(1)(t) lists discipline elsewhere for substantially the same reasons as a ground.
Then read 247 CMR 10.03(3), which is expressed to operate notwithstanding the grounds for discipline specified in 247 CMR 10.03, so it displaces a listed ground rather than competing with it.

Follow the carve-out to its second limb, which covers not only providing or assisting in providing, or dispensing medication for, the protected services, but any conviction, judgment, discipline, or other sanction arising from such health care services.

Test the two qualifiers, both of which must hold: that the services provided would have been lawful in Massachusetts, and that they are consistent with standards for good professional practice in Massachusetts. On these facts both are satisfied.
worked_examples.resolution: Discipline may not be imposed on this basis, because the carve-out reaches the foreign sanction itself and not only the underlying care. The error the scenario invites is stopping at the listed ground, when the provision that decides the question is written to override the whole grounds list.

quick_review.text: 247 CMR 10.01 lists the credentials the Board may discipline: a registered pharmacist, a pharmacy technician, a pharmacy, a pharmacy department, a wholesale license, and/or a controlled substance registration issued by the Board.
247 CMR 10.03(1) allows disciplinary action against an individual or entity licensed or registered by the Board, so individual and entity credentials are reached by the same provision.

The grounds available are those listed in M.G.L. c. 112, § 61 or those listed in 247 CMR 10.03, and 247 CMR 10.03(2) preserves the Board's adoption of policies and grounds through adjudication as well as through rulemaking.
247 CMR 10.03(1)(f) reaches conduct beyond the authorized scope of a pharmacist, pharmacy intern or pharmacy technician.

247 CMR 10.03(1)(g) reaches practising while the ability to practise is impaired by illness, use of alcohol, drugs, chemicals or any other type of substance, or by any mental or physical condition, and 247 CMR 10.03(1)(h) separately reaches abuse or illegal use of prescription drugs or controlled substances.

247 CMR 10.03(1)(i) reaches continuing to practise after a registration is lapsed, suspended or revoked, and 247 CMR 10.03(1)(m) reaches knowingly permitting, aiding or abetting an unlicensed person to perform activities requiring a license or registration.

247 CMR 10.02 defines conviction to include a guilty verdict or finding of guilt, an admission to or finding of sufficient facts regardless of adjudication, a continuance without a finding, and a plea of guilty or nolo contendere, of or to a crime in any jurisdiction accepted by the court, whether or not a sentence has been imposed.
A conviction of a person licensed or registered by the Board is conclusive evidence of the commission of that crime in any disciplinary proceeding against that person based upon the conviction.
247 CMR 10.06(7) allows out-of-state discipline to be the basis for initiation by the Board only where the conduct disciplined there constitutes a violation of Massachusetts law.
247 CMR 10.03(1)(t) makes having been disciplined in another jurisdiction in any way for reasons substantially the same as those in 247 CMR 10.03 a ground in its own right.

247 CMR 10.03(1)(q) makes failing without cause to cooperate an independent ground, covering a request to appear, requested information, a Board subpoena, and records, documents, information or testimony to which the Board is legally entitled.

247 CMR 10.03(3) operates notwithstanding the grounds specified in 247 CMR 10.03, and shields both the protected reproductive or gender-affirming health care services and any conviction, judgment, discipline or other sanction arising from them.

decision_logic.condition: A complaint arrives and the question is what the Board may act against.
decision_logic.action: List the credentials in play against 247 CMR 10.01, remembering that it names entity credentials as well as individual ones, and that 247 CMR 10.03(1) reaches an individual or entity licensed or registered by the Board.

decision_logic.condition: The conduct described does not match any lettered ground in 247 CMR 10.03.
decision_logic.action: Do not conclude that no ground exists. 247 CMR 10.03(1) also opens onto the grounds listed in M.G.L. c. 112, § 61, and 247 CMR 10.03(2) preserves grounds developed through adjudication.

decision_logic.condition: Someone performed work that requires a license or registration and was not authorised to do it.
decision_logic.action: Separate the actor from the person who permitted the act. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(f) addresses conduct beyond the authorized scope of the role, and 247 CMR 10.03(1)(m) addresses knowingly permitting, aiding or abetting.

decision_logic.condition: The facts include impairment, or use of alcohol or of a controlled substance, but no dispensing error.
decision_logic.action: Apply 247 CMR 10.03(1)(g) and (h) on their own terms. Neither provision states an element of patient harm or of an error occurring.

decision_logic.condition: A criminal matter is said not to be a conviction because of how it was resolved.
decision_logic.action: Match the resolution against the definition in 247 CMR 10.02 before accepting the characterisation, and check whether the proceeding before the Board is one based upon the conviction, in which case the conviction is conclusive evidence of the crime.

decision_logic.condition: Another state or jurisdiction has already disciplined the licensee.
decision_logic.action: Ask whether the conduct disciplined there constitutes a violation of Massachusetts law, which is the proviso in 247 CMR 10.06(7), and separately whether the reasons were substantially the same as those in 247 CMR 10.03 for the purposes of 247 CMR 10.03(1)(t).

decision_logic.condition: The conduct in question is, or arises from, reproductive or gender-affirming health care services.
decision_logic.action: Apply 247 CMR 10.03(3) before working through the grounds list, and check both qualifiers: that the services would have been lawful in Massachusetts and that they are consistent with standards for good professional practice in Massachusetts.

decision_logic.condition: A licensee has not responded to a Board request, a subpoena, or a demand for records.
decision_logic.action: Treat that as its own question under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(q) rather than folding it into the underlying complaint, and ask only whether the failure was without cause.

exceptions.text: 247 CMR 10.03(3) operates notwithstanding the grounds for discipline specified in 247 CMR 10.03, so it displaces those grounds rather than being weighed against them.

The protection in 247 CMR 10.03(3) is conditional: it holds so long as the services provided would have been lawful in Massachusetts and are consistent with standards for good professional practice in Massachusetts.

The out-of-state basis in 247 CMR 10.06(7) is available only where the conduct disciplined in the other state or jurisdiction constitutes a violation of Massachusetts law, and only where that person is also registered or licensed there.
The cooperation ground in 247 CMR 10.03(1)(q) applies to a failure without cause, so the provision itself contemplates that a failure may be excused where cause exists.

forms_records.text: 247 CMR 10.03(1)(q) names the material the Board is entitled to receive: records, documents, information or testimony, furnished to the Board, its investigators or representatives.
A Board subpoena is listed in 247 CMR 10.03(1)(q) separately from a request to appear or to provide requested information, so failing to respond to a subpoena is covered in its own right.

role_duties.duty: Practise within the authorized scope of a pharmacist, and not practise while the ability to practise is impaired or after a registration is lapsed, suspended or revoked.

Refrain from knowingly permitting, aiding or abetting an unlicensed person to perform activities requiring a license or registration, since that is a ground against the permitting licensee personally.
Stay within the authorized scope of the role, which 247 CMR 10.03(1)(f) names alongside that of the pharmacist.
Hold credentials that 247 CMR 10.01 lists as subject to Board disciplinary action, separately from the individuals working within them.

role_duties.role: Holder of a wholesale license or of a controlled substance registration issued by the Board
role_duties.duty: Hold a credential named in 247 CMR 10.01 as one the Board may take disciplinary action against.

role_duties.role: Any registrant or licensee who receives a Board request
role_duties.duty: Cooperate with a request to appear or to provide information, respond to a Board subpoena, and furnish the Board, its investigators or representatives with records, documents, information or testimony to which the Board is legally entitled.

role_duties.role: Massachusetts registrant or licensee also registered or licensed elsewhere
role_duties.duty: Understand that discipline imposed in that other jurisdiction may support Massachusetts action where the conduct disciplined constitutes a violation of Massachusetts law.

role_duties.role: Licensee who provides, assists in providing, or dispenses medication for protected health care services
role_duties.duty: Fall within 247 CMR 10.03(3), which bars discipline for those services and for any conviction, judgment, discipline or other sanction arising from them, subject to the two stated qualifiers.

common_traps.text: Reading the lettered grounds in 247 CMR 10.03 as an exhaustive list. The same provision opens onto M.G.L. c. 112, § 61, and 247 CMR 10.03(2) preserves grounds adopted through adjudication.
Assuming a single episode can produce only a single disciplinary matter. 247 CMR 10.01 lists individual and entity credentials together, and nothing there requires the Board to elect between them.
Assuming the Board reaches only people. A pharmacy, a pharmacy department, a wholesale license and a Board-issued controlled substance registration are each named in 247 CMR 10.01.
Treating a good outcome as curing a scope violation. Neither 247 CMR 10.03(1)(f) nor 247 CMR 10.03(1)(m) states an element of patient harm.
Assuming that only the person who performed an out-of-scope act is exposed. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(m) is addressed to the licensee who knowingly permits, aids or abets.
Reading the impairment ground as requiring drugs or alcohol. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(g) also names illness and any mental or physical condition.
Concluding that a continuance without a finding, a withheld adjudication, or the absence of a sentence means there is no conviction. 247 CMR 10.02 names each of those inside the definition.
Attempting to reargue the underlying facts of a crime before the Board. Under 247 CMR 10.02 the conviction is conclusive evidence of the commission of that crime in a proceeding based upon it.
Treating discipline in another jurisdiction as automatically actionable here. 247 CMR 10.06(7) conditions the basis on the conduct disciplined there constituting a violation of Massachusetts law.
Believing that winning the underlying complaint disposes of a failure to respond to the Board. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(q) is a listed ground standing on its own.

Placing 247 CMR 10.03(3) alongside the other grounds and balancing them. It is expressed to operate notwithstanding those grounds, and it reaches the foreign conviction, judgment, discipline or sanction as well as the care itself.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 10.03(1) grounds for discipline include engaging in conduct beyond the authorized scope of a pharmacist, pharmacy intern or pharmacy technician; practising the profession while the ability to practise is impaired by illness, use of alcohol, drugs, chemicals or any other substance, or as a result of any mental or physical condition; engaging in abuse or illegal use of prescription drugs or controlled substances; continuing to practise after a registration is lapsed, suspended or revoked; and knowingly permitting, aiding or abetting an unlicensed person to perform activities requiring a licence or registration.

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 10.02 conviction includes any guilty verdict or finding of guilt and any admission to or finding of sufficient facts to warrant a finding of guilt, regardless of adjudication, a continuance without a finding, and any plea of guilty or nolo contendere, of or to a crime in any jurisdiction, which has been accepted by the court, whether or not a sentence has been imposed. A conviction of any person licensed or registered by the Board is conclusive evidence of the commission of that crime in any disciplinary proceeding based upon the conviction.

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 10.06(7) disciplinary action taken against a Massachusetts registrant or licensee by another state or jurisdiction in which that person is also registered may be the basis for the Board initiating disciplinary action, provided that the conduct disciplined in the other jurisdiction constitutes a violation of Massachusetts law. Under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(t) having been disciplined in another jurisdiction for reasons substantially the same as those in 247 CMR 10.03 is itself a ground for discipline.

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(q) it is an independent ground for discipline to fail, without cause, to cooperate with any request by the Board to appear before it or to provide requested information, to fail to respond to a Board subpoena, or to fail to furnish the Board, its investigators or representatives with records, documents, information or testimony to which the Board is legally entitled.

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 10.03(3), notwithstanding the grounds for discipline in 247 CMR 10.03, no licensee shall be subject to discipline for providing or assisting in providing, or dispensing medication for, reproductive health care services or gender-affirming health care services as defined at M.G.L. c. 12, § 11I½, or for any conviction, judgment, discipline or other sanction arising from such health care services, so long as the services provided would have been lawful in Massachusetts and are consistent with standards for good professional practice in Massachusetts.

orientation.text: A Massachusetts disciplinary matter has a defined beginning, a Board choice in the middle, and a small set of possible endings, and 247 CMR 10.00 supplies all three. It begins with a complaint, and 247 CMR 10.02 defines that word narrowly: a complaint is a communication filed with the Board or the Division of Health Professions Licensure which the Board determines, after investigation, merits further consideration or action. The Board's determination is therefore part of the definition rather than something that happens to a complaint later. A letter of grievance is a communication on the day it arrives; it becomes a complaint when the Board, having investigated, decides it merits further consideration or action. 247 CMR 10.05 then gives the Board its choice: after receipt of a complaint and all related investigative materials the Board may schedule an investigative conference, or may schedule a formal adjudicatory hearing pursuant to M.G.L. c. 30A and 801 CMR 1.01 if it determines that one is required.

The two tracks differ in formality and in the document that opens them. An investigative conference is defined at 247 CMR 10.02 as an informal discussion relating to a complaint held with the Board, and under 247 CMR 10.04 the Board may schedule one at any time prior to the commencement of a formal adjudicatory proceeding, giving timely notice which shall include a general statement of the nature of the issues to be discussed. An adjudicatory hearing is a formal administrative hearing held by the Board to determine the truth and validity of complaints filed against a registrant or licensee, conducted pursuant to M.G.L. c. 30A and 801 CMR 1.01. The instrument that summons a registrant to it is the Order to Show Cause, which 247 CMR 10.02 defines as a document served by the Board upon a registrant ordering the registrant or licensee to appear before the Board for a formal adjudicatory hearing. Because 247 CMR 10.04 makes the conference available at any time before a formal proceeding commences and 247 CMR 10.05 offers the two as alternatives, the informal conference is an option the Board holds and not a gateway the Board has to pass through.

What the Board may do at the end is a list in 247 CMR 10.06, and the list is only loosely a ladder, because its first two items are not discipline at all. Dismissal of the complaint comes first. The second is the advisory letter, an official written document retained in the Board's files delineating the Board's concerns with the registrant's or licensee's professional practice, and the regulation states in terms that an advisory letter does not constitute formal disciplinary action. From the third item onward the actions are formal. A reprimand constitutes formal disciplinary action, and a censure is a severe reprimand, so a censure is the heavier of the pair rather than a separate lesser category. Probation constitutes disciplinary action and consists of a period of time during which the registrant or licensee may practise under conditions imposed by the Board pursuant to a formal adjudicatory hearing or consent agreement, which makes it the one formal sanction that leaves the registrant working. Suspension or revocation of a personal registration, pharmacy permit, licence or controlled substance registration may be imposed pursuant to a decision and order of the Board following a formal adjudicatory hearing or following the execution of a consent agreement. The list in 247 CMR 10.06 continues past these items; what may be disciplined, and whose credentials the Board reaches, belongs to the companion section on grounds and is not taught here.

Not every restriction waits for the end of the process, and the two instruments that do not wait are easy to confuse because both answer an immediate or serious threat. 247 CMR 10.07 permits the Board, where it determines on affidavits or other documentary evidence that a licensee is an immediate or serious threat to the public health, safety or welfare, to suspend or refuse to renew a licence pending a final hearing on the merits of the allegations, and it fixes the price of acting that early: a hearing limited to the determination of the necessity of the summary action shall be afforded the licensee within seven days of the Board's action. 247 CMR 10.08 supplies a second and different instrument. Where the Board or Board President determines on affidavits or other evidence that a registrant or licensee, or the products prepared by a registrant or licensee, are an immediate or serious threat, a Cease and Desist Notice or Quarantine Notice may issue, and what such a notice imposes is expressly a non-disciplinary cessation or restriction of pharmacy operations, or a non-disciplinary restriction on the registrant or licensee to the extent necessary to avert a continued threat pending final investigation results. The hearing clock attached to a notice is 15 business days, not seven days, and under 247 CMR 10.08(2) the requirements of the notice remain in effect until the Board or Board President rescinds or amends them, or until the Board takes final action on any related pending complaint and issues a final decision.

The deadlines that fall on the licensee rather than on the Board sit in a different part of the regulation and are not hearing clocks at all. They appear in 247 CMR 10.03(1), which is the list of grounds for discipline, so missing one of them is itself something the Board may discipline for. Under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(y) it is a ground for discipline to fail to report, or to fail to report accurately, to the Board within seven business days, in a manner and format determined by the Board, discipline under 247 CMR 10.06 on the basis of actions listed in 247 CMR 10.03(1). Under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(z) the same seven business days runs on any final action, including licence surrender or resignation, regarding a registrant or licensee by any other governmental authority in this state or another jurisdiction, and the subsection expressly reaches action against any other health care related professional registration or licence the person holds, so an out-of-state sanction on a nursing or medical credential is caught by it. Under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(aa) a pending criminal charge or conviction, in Massachusetts or any other jurisdiction, is reported to the Board in writing within 30 days. Seven days and seven business days are not the same period, and in this area the one measured in business days is the licensee's while the one measured in plain days is the Board's.

A matter can end without an adjudicatory hearing, and 247 CMR 10.06(6) is how. A consent agreement is a resolution of a complaint agreed upon by the Board and the registrant or licensee which may contain conditions placed by the Board on the registrant's or licensee's professional conduct and practice, and which may include the voluntary suspension or surrender of a personal registration, pharmacy permit, licence or controlled substance registration, permanently or for a fixed period of time. Surrender inside such an agreement is not an informal exit from a difficult file. The voluntary surrender agreement shall be in writing and be signed by the registrant or licensee and the Board; shall recite the facts upon which it is based and include, but not be limited to, provisions addressing reinstatement and any conditions the Board may elect to impose; shall state that the registrant or licensee realises that the surrender is an act which deprives him or her of all privileges of registration and is not subject to judicial review; and shall be placed in the registrant's or licensee's Board file as part of the permanent Board records. The consent agreement is also one of the two routes by which probation, suspension and revocation may be imposed under 247 CMR 10.06(4) and (5), the other being a formal adjudicatory hearing, so the negotiated ending and the adjudicated ending can arrive at the same sanction by different paths.

The last period in this area runs after the sanction rather than during the process. 247 CMR 4.02(6) provides that an applicant for personal registration renewal whose personal registration has been revoked or has been suspended for between six months and two years shall take and pass the Multistate Pharmacy Jurisprudence Examination and meet all conditions as determined by the Board as a prerequisite to registration renewal. 247 CMR 4.02(7) provides that an applicant whose personal registration has been revoked or suspended for more than two years shall take and pass the MPJE and meet all other conditions as determined by the Board, which may include taking and passing the NAPLEX, as a prerequisite to registration renewal. The MPJE is therefore common to both tiers and settles nothing between them; the NAPLEX is named only in the longer tier, and even there it is named as something the Board's conditions may include rather than as an automatic requirement. Two boundaries are worth fixing. This is the ladder for a registration that was suspended or revoked, and a registration that merely lapsed without ever being suspended or revoked returns by a different route which this section does not teach. And neither subsection states a requirement for a suspension shorter than six months, so nothing here should be applied to one.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist receives written notice that the Board has scheduled an investigative conference about a complaint concerning her dispensing records. The notice contains a general statement of the nature of the issues to be discussed. Her employer's counsel tells her that the conference is the first mandatory step of a hearing sequence, that a formal adjudicatory hearing can only follow it, and that the notice is effectively an Order to Show Cause. She asks what the conference actually is and what it is not.
steps: Start with what the regulation calls it. 247 CMR 10.02 defines an investigative conference as an informal discussion relating to a complaint held with the Board, which is a different thing from the formal administrative hearing that 247 CMR 10.02 defines as an adjudicatory hearing.

Check when it may be scheduled. Under 247 CMR 10.04 the Board may schedule an investigative conference at any time prior to the commencement of a formal adjudicatory proceeding, and shall give timely notice including a general statement of the nature of the issues to be discussed, which is what she has received.

Check whether it is mandatory. 247 CMR 10.05 provides that after receipt of a complaint and all related investigative materials the Board may schedule an investigative conference or may schedule a formal adjudicatory hearing, so the two are alternatives and the conference is not a prerequisite.

Identify the document that does open the formal track. An Order to Show Cause is defined at 247 CMR 10.02 as a document served by the Board upon a registrant ordering the registrant or licensee to appear before the Board for a formal adjudicatory hearing, which this notice is not.

Note what has already happened before either track opens. Her file became a complaint within the meaning of 247 CMR 10.02 only when the Board determined, after investigation, that the communication merited further consideration or action.
worked_examples.resolution: The conference is an informal discussion the Board has elected to hold, it is not a required gateway to a formal hearing, and the notice is not an Order to Show Cause. The error the scenario invites is treating the stages of 247 CMR 10.00 as a fixed sequence every matter must climb, when 247 CMR 10.05 gives the Board a choice between the informal and the formal track after investigation.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacist also holds a nursing licence in a neighbouring state. On a Monday that state's nursing board enters a final action against the nursing licence. Eleven days later she is criminally charged in Massachusetts with an offence unrelated to her practice. She decides to wait until the criminal case is resolved and then report both matters together, on the view that the nursing action is not a pharmacy matter and that an unproved charge is nothing to report.
steps: Locate the duties. Both sit in 247 CMR 10.03(1), the list of grounds for discipline, so a failure to report is itself a ground on which the Board may discipline her.

Take the out-of-state action first. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(z) requires report to the Board, in a manner and format determined by the Board, within seven business days of any final action, including licence surrender or resignation, regarding a registrant or licensee by any other governmental authority in this state or another jurisdiction.

Answer the objection that it is not a pharmacy matter. The same subsection expressly reaches action against any other health care related professional registration or licence held by the registrant or licensee, so the nursing action is within it.

Take the criminal charge second. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(aa) requires report to the Board, in writing, within 30 days of any pending criminal charge or conviction, in Massachusetts or any other jurisdiction, so the duty attaches while the charge is pending rather than on any adjudication.

Notice that the two clocks are different in length, in unit and in the form the report takes: seven business days in a manner and format determined by the Board for the final action, and 30 days in writing for the criminal charge, each running from its own trigger.
worked_examples.resolution: Two separate reports were due on two separate clocks, the earlier one within seven business days of the out-of-state final action and the later one in writing within 30 days of the charge. The error the scenario invites is bundling reportable events into a single later report, with a second error behind it: reading the reporting duties as confined to pharmacy credentials and to concluded criminal cases.

worked_examples.scenario: Board investigators find that a pharmacy's compounded preparations may be contaminated. On the same day the Board President issues a Quarantine Notice prohibiting use of the medications in the pharmacy's possession, and the Board separately determines on affidavits that the supervising pharmacist is an immediate or serious threat and suspends that pharmacist's licence pending a final hearing. The pharmacy's counsel prepares one calendar entry, on the view that both actions are emergency discipline governed by a single seven-day review period.
steps: Separate the two instruments. The action against the pharmacist is a suspension prior to hearing under 247 CMR 10.07; the action against the preparations is a Quarantine Notice of the kind 247 CMR 10.08(1) permits the Board or Board President to issue.
Date the first clock. Under 247 CMR 10.07 a hearing limited to the determination of the necessity of the summary action shall be afforded the licensee within seven days of the Board's action.

Date the second clock separately. Under 247 CMR 10.08(3) a hearing limited to the determination of the necessity of the notice shall be afforded within 15 business days of the Board's or Board President's action, so the two entries do not coincide.

Fix the character of each action. The suspension is a summary action against a licence pending a final hearing on the merits; what a Cease and Desist Notice or Quarantine Notice imposes is expressly a non-disciplinary cessation or restriction pending final investigation results.
Note who may act. 247 CMR 10.07 speaks of the Board, while 247 CMR 10.08(1) and the notices in 247 CMR 10.06(8) and (9) may issue from the Board or the Board President.

Note when the notice ends. Under 247 CMR 10.08(2) its requirements remain in effect until the Board or Board President rescinds or amends them, or until the Board takes final action on any related pending complaint and issues a final decision.
worked_examples.resolution: Two hearing clocks run, seven days on the pharmacist's summary suspension and 15 business days on the Quarantine Notice, and only the first is action against a licence. The error the scenario invites is collapsing the two pre-hearing mechanisms of 247 CMR 10.07 and 10.08 into one, which also produces the further mistake of calling a notice that the regulation describes as imposing non-disciplinary restrictions a form of emergency discipline.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist negotiating with the Board signs a consent agreement under which she voluntarily surrenders her personal registration for a fixed period of eighteen months, with conditions attached. Fourteen months in she regrets the bargain, and asks whether she can take the surrender to court, and what she will need to do at the end of the period to be renewed. She assumes the surrender is simply a pause and that serving out the period restores her.
steps: Establish what she signed. Under 247 CMR 10.06(6) a consent agreement is a resolution of a complaint agreed upon by the Board and the registrant which may contain conditions placed by the Board on professional conduct and practice, and which may include voluntary suspension or surrender, permanently or for a fixed period of time.

Read the terms the surrender agreement must carry. It shall be in writing and signed by the registrant and the Board, shall recite the facts upon which it is based and include provisions addressing reinstatement and any conditions the Board may elect to impose, and shall be placed in her Board file as part of the permanent Board records.

Answer the question about court. The agreement shall state that the registrant realises that the surrender is an act which deprives her of all privileges of registration and is not subject to judicial review, so the waiver is a term of the document she signed rather than an argument to be made later.

Answer the question about coming back. Eighteen months sits between six months and two years, so 247 CMR 4.02(6) governs: an applicant for personal registration renewal whose registration has been revoked or suspended for between six months and two years shall take and pass the MPJE and meet all conditions as determined by the Board as a prerequisite to renewal.

Check whether the NAPLEX enters. It does not on these facts; taking and passing the NAPLEX appears only in 247 CMR 4.02(7), among the Board's other conditions where the registration has been revoked or suspended for more than two years.

Keep the two sets of conditions distinct. The conditions in her consent agreement and the conditions the Board determines under 247 CMR 4.02(6) are separate requirements, and the agreement's own reinstatement provisions do not displace the renewal prerequisites.
worked_examples.resolution: The surrender is not reviewable by a court because the agreement had to say so, and serving the eighteen months does not renew her: she must take and pass the MPJE and meet all conditions the Board determines. The error the scenario invites is reading a negotiated surrender as a reversible pause, and behind it the assumption that the end of the sanction period is itself the route back to practice.

worked_examples.scenario: Three pharmacists in one chain describe their Board outcomes to each other. The first received an advisory letter after a complaint was reviewed. The second was placed on probation under a consent agreement and told to stop work at once. The third received a censure and takes comfort in it, on the view that a censure is a gentler finding than a reprimand. Each of them is wrong about something.
steps: Classify the first outcome. Under 247 CMR 10.06(2) an advisory letter is an official written document retained in the Board's files delineating the Board's concerns with the registrant's professional practice, and the regulation states that an advisory letter does not constitute formal disciplinary action.
Do not push that too far. The letter is retained in the Board's files, so it is not the same thing as no outcome at all; what it is not is formal disciplinary action.

Classify the second outcome. Under 247 CMR 10.06(4) probation constitutes disciplinary action and consists of a period of time during which the registrant may practise under conditions imposed by the Board, so probation is discipline that permits continued practice rather than a stoppage.

Identify the source of the second pharmacist's probation. 247 CMR 10.06(4) names both a formal adjudicatory hearing and a consent agreement as the routes by which probation may be imposed, so arriving there by agreement changes nothing about its character.
Classify the third outcome. Under 247 CMR 10.06(3) a reprimand constitutes formal disciplinary action and a censure is a severe reprimand, so a censure is the heavier of the two.
worked_examples.resolution: The advisory letter is not formal discipline but is retained in Board files, probation is formal discipline that expressly permits practice under conditions, and a censure is a severe reprimand rather than a lighter one. The error the scenario invites is ranking Board outcomes by how the words sound rather than by the classification 247 CMR 10.06 attaches to each of them.

Seven business days is the registrant's or licensee's period to report discipline under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(y) and any final action by another governmental authority under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(z).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pending criminal charge is reported to the Board within ______ and in what form?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 30 days, in writing, under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(aa); the duty attaches while the charge is pending and does not wait for a conviction.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: an out-of-state final action against a pharmacist's nursing licence is outside the Board's reporting duties because it is not a pharmacy matter.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(z) reaches any final action by any other governmental authority in this state or another jurisdiction, expressly including action against any other health care related professional registration or licence the person holds, within seven business days.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: When does a communication become a complaint within the meaning of 247 CMR 10.02?
retrieval_prompts.answer: When the Board determines, after investigation, that the communication filed with the Board or the Division of Health Professions Licensure merits further consideration or action.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: an investigative conference must be held before the Board may schedule a formal adjudicatory hearing.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Under 247 CMR 10.05 the Board may schedule an investigative conference or a formal adjudicatory hearing after receipt of a complaint and investigative materials, and 247 CMR 10.04 makes the conference available at any time prior to the commencement of a formal adjudicatory proceeding.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which document orders a registrant to appear before the Board for a formal adjudicatory hearing, and how does 247 CMR 10.02 describe it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The Order to Show Cause, a document served by the Board upon a registrant ordering the registrant or licensee to appear before the Board for a formal adjudicatory hearing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Of dismissal, advisory letter, reprimand, censure, probation and revocation, which do not constitute formal disciplinary action?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Dismissal of the complaint and the advisory letter. 247 CMR 10.06(2) states that an advisory letter does not constitute formal disciplinary action, although it is an official written document retained in the Board's files.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which formal sanction in 247 CMR 10.06 permits the registrant to keep practising, and on what terms?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Probation. It constitutes disciplinary action and consists of a period of time during which the registrant or licensee may practise under conditions imposed by the Board pursuant to a formal adjudicatory hearing or consent agreement.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the four things a voluntary surrender agreement shall do under 247 CMR 10.06(6).
retrieval_prompts.answer: Be in writing and signed by the registrant or licensee and the Board; recite the facts upon which it is based and include provisions addressing reinstatement and any conditions the Board may elect to impose; state that the registrant or licensee realises the surrender deprives him or her of all privileges of registration and is not subject to judicial review; and be placed in the Board file as part of the permanent Board records.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A consent agreement may include voluntary suspension or surrender for how long?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Permanently or for a fixed period of time, under 247 CMR 10.06(6).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A registration was suspended for nine months. Which subsection governs renewal, and what does it require?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 4.02(6), because nine months falls between six months and two years. The applicant shall take and pass the MPJE and meet all conditions as determined by the Board as a prerequisite to registration renewal; the NAPLEX is not named in that subsection.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What is the only thing that changes between 247 CMR 4.02(6) and 247 CMR 4.02(7)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Both require taking and passing the MPJE and meeting the conditions the Board determines. Only 4.02(7), which reaches a registration revoked or suspended for more than two years, adds that those conditions may include taking and passing the NAPLEX.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a Cease and Desist Notice is a form of emergency discipline.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. What the notice imposes under 247 CMR 10.08(1) is expressly a non-disciplinary cessation or restriction of pharmacy operations, or a non-disciplinary restriction on the registrant or licensee, pending final investigation results.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long do the requirements of a Cease and Desist Notice or Quarantine Notice remain in effect?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Until the Board or Board President rescinds or amends them, or until the Board takes final action on any related pending complaint and issues a final decision, under 247 CMR 10.08(2).

quick_review.text: A complaint under 247 CMR 10.02 is a communication filed with the Board or the Division of Health Professions Licensure which the Board determines, after investigation, merits further consideration or action.

An investigative conference is an informal discussion relating to a complaint held with the Board; an adjudicatory hearing is a formal administrative hearing under M.G.L. c. 30A and 801 CMR 1.01; an Order to Show Cause is the document served by the Board ordering the registrant to appear for that hearing.

Under 247 CMR 10.04 the Board may schedule an investigative conference at any time prior to the commencement of a formal adjudicatory proceeding, on timely notice including a general statement of the nature of the issues; under 247 CMR 10.05 it may schedule either a conference or a formal hearing after receiving the complaint and investigative materials.
247 CMR 10.06 lists the actions available to the Board, beginning with dismissal of the complaint and the advisory letter, which does not constitute formal disciplinary action.

A reprimand constitutes formal disciplinary action and a censure is a severe reprimand; probation constitutes disciplinary action and permits practice under Board-imposed conditions; suspension or revocation follows a decision and order after a formal adjudicatory hearing or the execution of a consent agreement.

Under 247 CMR 10.07 the Board may suspend or refuse to renew a licence pending a final hearing where affidavits or other documentary evidence show the licensee is an immediate or serious threat, and a hearing limited to the necessity of that action is afforded within seven days.

Under 247 CMR 10.08 the Board or Board President may issue a Cease and Desist Notice or Quarantine Notice imposing non-disciplinary cessation or restriction, with a hearing limited to its necessity within 15 business days, and the notice stands until rescinded or amended or until the Board issues a final decision on a related pending complaint.

Summary cease-and-desist and quarantine authority exists so the Board can act before a final adjudicatory hearing where operations or products are an immediate and serious threat, and the regulation's own review procedures continue to apply.

247 CMR 10.03(1)(y) and (z) make it a ground for discipline to fail to report, or to report inaccurately, within seven business days, in a manner and format determined by the Board, discipline under 247 CMR 10.06 on the basis of actions listed in 247 CMR 10.03(1), and any final action, including licence surrender or resignation, by any other governmental authority in this state or another jurisdiction.
247 CMR 10.03(1)(aa) separately requires report to the Board, in writing, within 30 days of any pending criminal charge or conviction in Massachusetts or any other jurisdiction.

A consent agreement under 247 CMR 10.06(6) resolves a complaint by agreement between the Board and the registrant or licensee, may impose conditions on professional conduct and practice, and may include voluntary suspension or surrender permanently or for a fixed period.

A voluntary surrender agreement is written and signed, recites the facts, addresses reinstatement and any Board conditions, states that the surrender deprives the registrant of all privileges of registration and is not subject to judicial review, and is placed in the permanent Board records.
Under 247 CMR 4.02(6) a registration revoked, or suspended for between six months and two years, is renewed only on taking and passing the MPJE and meeting all conditions the Board determines.

Under 247 CMR 4.02(7) a registration revoked or suspended for more than two years is renewed only on taking and passing the MPJE and meeting all other Board conditions, which may include taking and passing the NAPLEX.

decision_logic.condition: A communication about a registrant has arrived at the Board and someone asks whether a complaint is pending.
decision_logic.action: Ask whether the Board has determined, after investigation, that the communication merits further consideration or action. Until it has, the definition in 247 CMR 10.02 is not satisfied.

decision_logic.condition: The Board has a complaint and all related investigative materials in hand.
decision_logic.action: Expect a choice rather than a sequence: under 247 CMR 10.05 the Board may schedule an investigative conference or may schedule a formal adjudicatory hearing if it determines that one is required. Do not treat the conference as a mandatory first step.

decision_logic.condition: A registrant has been notified of a Board proceeding and needs to know how formal it is.
decision_logic.action: Read the notice. A notice of an investigative conference with a general statement of the nature of the issues signals the informal track under 247 CMR 10.04; an Order to Show Cause signals a formal adjudicatory hearing under M.G.L. c. 30A and 801 CMR 1.01.

decision_logic.condition: A Board outcome has to be classified as discipline or not.
decision_logic.action: Place it in 247 CMR 10.06. Dismissal and the advisory letter are not formal disciplinary action; reprimand, censure, probation, suspension and revocation are. A Cease and Desist or Quarantine Notice imposes restrictions the regulation calls non-disciplinary.

decision_logic.condition: The Board has acted before any final hearing and a review date has to be diarised.
decision_logic.action: Identify the instrument first. A suspension or refusal to renew under 247 CMR 10.07 carries a hearing on its necessity within seven days of the Board's action; a Cease and Desist or Quarantine Notice carries one within 15 business days of the Board's or Board President's action under 247 CMR 10.08(3).

decision_logic.condition: Something reportable has happened to a registrant or licensee.
decision_logic.action: Ask what kind of event it is. Discipline under 247 CMR 10.06 on the basis of actions listed in 247 CMR 10.03(1), and any final action by another governmental authority, run on seven business days in a manner and format determined by the Board; a pending criminal charge or conviction runs on 30 days and must be in writing.

decision_logic.condition: A registrant wants the matter to end without a formal adjudicatory hearing.
decision_logic.action: Look to a consent agreement under 247 CMR 10.06(6). It can carry Board conditions on professional conduct and practice, and can include voluntary suspension or surrender permanently or for a fixed period, but a surrender must contain the terms 247 CMR 10.06(6) prescribes, including the statement that it is not subject to judicial review.

decision_logic.condition: A registration that was suspended or revoked is up for renewal.
decision_logic.action: Measure the sanction. Between six months and two years puts the applicant in 247 CMR 4.02(6): MPJE plus all conditions the Board determines. More than two years puts the applicant in 247 CMR 4.02(7): MPJE plus all other Board conditions, which may include the NAPLEX.

decision_logic.condition: A registration was never suspended or revoked but has not been renewed.
decision_logic.action: Do not use 247 CMR 4.02(6) or (7). Those subsections govern registrations that were revoked or suspended; a simple failure to renew follows a different route back, which is outside this section.

exceptions.text: The advisory letter is the carve-out inside the list of Board actions: it is an official written document retained in the Board's files, and 247 CMR 10.06(2) states that it does not constitute formal disciplinary action.
Probation is the exception to the assumption that formal discipline stops practice: it consists of a period during which the registrant or licensee may practise under conditions imposed by the Board.

What a Cease and Desist Notice or Quarantine Notice imposes under 247 CMR 10.08(1) is expressly non-disciplinary, which is what separates it from the summary suspension in 247 CMR 10.07 even though both answer an immediate or serious threat.

A voluntary surrender agreement carries an express waiver: it shall state that the registrant or licensee realises the surrender is an act which deprives him or her of all privileges of registration and is not subject to judicial review.

The NAPLEX is not a general reinstatement requirement. It is named only in 247 CMR 4.02(7), and there only among the other conditions the Board may determine, for a registration revoked or suspended for more than two years.
Neither 247 CMR 4.02(6) nor 247 CMR 4.02(7) states a requirement for a suspension of less than six months, so neither tier should be applied to one.

timing_deadlines.event: The Board suspends or refuses to renew a licence prior to hearing under 247 CMR 10.07, on affidavits or other documentary evidence that the licensee is an immediate or serious threat to the public health, safety or welfare
timing_deadlines.timeframe: A hearing limited to the determination of the necessity of the summary action within seven days of the Board's action
timing_deadlines.consequence: The suspension or refusal to renew stands pending a final hearing on the merits, but the licensee is entitled to the necessity hearing inside seven days.

timing_deadlines.event: The Board or Board President issues a Cease and Desist Notice or Quarantine Notice under 247 CMR 10.06(8) and (9) or 247 CMR 10.08(1)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: A hearing limited to the determination of the necessity of the notice within 15 business days of the action
timing_deadlines.consequence: The registrant or licensee is entitled to a necessity hearing on a longer clock than the seven days that follows a summary suspension, and the restrictions imposed in the meantime are non-disciplinary.

timing_deadlines.event: A Cease and Desist Notice or Quarantine Notice is in force
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Until the Board or Board President rescinds or amends it, or until the Board takes final action on any related pending complaint and issues a final decision
timing_deadlines.consequence: The requirements of the notice continue to bind the registrant or licensee for that whole period under 247 CMR 10.08(2).

timing_deadlines.event: Discipline under 247 CMR 10.06 on the basis of actions listed in 247 CMR 10.03(1)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Report to the Board within seven business days, in a manner and format determined by the Board
timing_deadlines.consequence: Failing to report, or failing to report accurately, is itself a ground for discipline under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(y).

timing_deadlines.event: Any final action, including licence surrender or resignation, regarding a registrant or licensee by any other governmental authority in this state or another jurisdiction, including action against any other health care related professional registration or licence held
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Report to the Board within seven business days, in a manner and format determined by the Board
timing_deadlines.consequence: Failing to report is a ground for discipline under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(z), and the duty is not limited to pharmacy credentials.

timing_deadlines.event: A pending criminal charge or a conviction, in Massachusetts or any other jurisdiction
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Report to the Board in writing within 30 days
timing_deadlines.consequence: Failing to report is a ground for discipline under 247 CMR 10.03(1)(aa); the duty attaches while the charge is pending and does not wait for an adjudication.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Timely notice, given by the Board before the conference
timing_deadlines.consequence: The notice shall include a general statement of the nature of the issues to be discussed under 247 CMR 10.04.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: A period of time fixed by the Board, running from the formal adjudicatory hearing or consent agreement that imposes it
timing_deadlines.consequence: During that period the registrant or licensee may practise, but only under the conditions the Board imposes.

timing_deadlines.event: Voluntary suspension or surrender inside a consent agreement
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Permanent, or for a fixed period of time
timing_deadlines.consequence: For the duration the registrant or licensee is deprived of all privileges of registration, and the agreement's own reinstatement provisions govern what happens next.

timing_deadlines.event: A personal registration has been revoked, or suspended for between six months and two years
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The sanction band that selects 247 CMR 4.02(6)
timing_deadlines.consequence: The applicant shall take and pass the MPJE and meet all conditions as determined by the Board as a prerequisite to registration renewal.

timing_deadlines.event: A personal registration has been revoked or suspended for more than two years
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The sanction band that selects 247 CMR 4.02(7)
timing_deadlines.consequence: The applicant shall take and pass the MPJE and meet all other conditions as determined by the Board, which may include taking and passing the NAPLEX.

forms_records.text: The advisory letter is itself a record: an official written document retained in the Board's files delineating the Board's concerns with the registrant's or licensee's professional practice.
The Order to Show Cause is a document served by the Board upon a registrant ordering the registrant or licensee to appear before the Board for a formal adjudicatory hearing.
Notice of an investigative conference is given by the Board and shall include a general statement of the nature of the issues to be discussed.

A voluntary surrender agreement shall be in writing, be signed by the registrant or licensee and the Board, recite the facts upon which it is based, address reinstatement and any conditions the Board may elect to impose, and be placed in the registrant's or licensee's Board file as part of the permanent Board records.

Reports of discipline and of final action by another governmental authority are made to the Board in a manner and format determined by the Board; a report of a pending criminal charge or conviction is made in writing.
Suspension or revocation is recorded in a decision and order of the Board following a formal adjudicatory hearing, or in the executed consent agreement where that is the route taken.

Summary action rests on documentary material: 247 CMR 10.07 requires affidavits or other documentary evidence, and 247 CMR 10.08(1) affidavits or other evidence, before the Board or Board President acts.

role_duties.duty: Determine, after investigation, whether a communication merits further consideration or action, and then schedule either an investigative conference or a formal adjudicatory hearing.
Give timely notice of an investigative conference, including a general statement of the nature of the issues to be discussed.
Select an action from those available under 247 CMR 10.06, and impose probation, suspension or revocation only pursuant to a formal adjudicatory hearing or an executed consent agreement.
Afford a hearing limited to the necessity of a summary suspension or refusal to renew within seven days of its action under 247 CMR 10.07.

Issue, and afterwards rescind or amend, a Cease and Desist Notice or Quarantine Notice where a registrant, licensee or the products prepared by one are an immediate or serious threat, and afford a hearing on the necessity of the notice within 15 business days.

Report to the Board, within seven business days and in a manner and format determined by the Board, discipline under 247 CMR 10.06 on the basis of actions listed in 247 CMR 10.03(1), and any final action by any other governmental authority in this state or another jurisdiction.
Report to the Board in writing, within 30 days, any pending criminal charge or conviction in Massachusetts or any other jurisdiction.

role_duties.role: Registrant or licensee entering a consent agreement
role_duties.duty: Sign the agreement, accept the conditions the Board places on professional conduct and practice, and, where the agreement includes voluntary surrender, sign a document stating that the surrender deprives him or her of all privileges of registration and is not subject to judicial review.

role_duties.role: Applicant for renewal after suspension or revocation
role_duties.duty: Take and pass the MPJE and meet the conditions the Board determines, and expect the NAPLEX to become available to the Board as a further condition only where the registration was revoked or suspended for more than two years.

common_traps.text: Treating 247 CMR 10.00 as a fixed ladder every matter climbs. After receiving a complaint and investigative materials the Board may schedule an investigative conference or a formal adjudicatory hearing, and the conference is not a prerequisite to the hearing.

Treating any letter of grievance as a complaint. Under 247 CMR 10.02 a communication becomes a complaint only once the Board determines, after investigation, that it merits further consideration or action.

Reading an advisory letter as formal discipline because it is written and kept on file, or reading it as nothing at all because it is not discipline. It is an official written document retained in the Board's files which does not constitute formal disciplinary action.
Ranking censure below reprimand because the word sounds softer. A reprimand constitutes formal disciplinary action and a censure is a severe reprimand.
Assuming probation stops practice. Probation constitutes disciplinary action but consists of a period during which the registrant or licensee may practise under conditions imposed by the Board.

Running one clock for both pre-hearing mechanisms. A summary suspension or refusal to renew under 247 CMR 10.07 carries a seven-day necessity hearing; a Cease and Desist or Quarantine Notice carries 15 business days under 247 CMR 10.08(3).

Calling a Cease and Desist or Quarantine Notice emergency discipline. The cessation or restriction it imposes is described in the regulation as non-disciplinary, which is exactly what distinguishes it from action taken against a licence.

Confusing the two periods that are stated as seven. Seven days is the Board's clock to afford a necessity hearing; seven business days is the licensee's clock to report discipline or a final action by another governmental authority.

Waiting for a criminal case to conclude before reporting it, or bundling reportable events into one later report. 247 CMR 10.03(1)(aa) reaches a pending criminal charge and runs on 30 days, separately from the seven-business-day duties in 247 CMR 10.03(1)(y) and (z).

Reading a voluntary surrender as an informal exit that can be challenged later or simply waited out. The agreement must state that the surrender deprives the registrant of all privileges of registration and is not subject to judicial review, and it goes into the permanent Board records.

Assuming that serving out a suspension is itself the route back. Renewal after suspension or revocation requires taking and passing the MPJE and meeting the conditions the Board determines under 247 CMR 4.02(6) or (7).

Adding the NAPLEX to the shorter reinstatement tier. It is named only in 247 CMR 4.02(7), for a registration revoked or suspended for more than two years, and even there only among the conditions the Board may determine.

When pharmacy operations or products pose an immediate and serious threat to public health, safety, or welfare, the Board may use summary cease-and-desist or quarantine authority before a final adjudicatory hearing, subject to the regulation's review procedures.
